title: A socket is a file descriptor
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why the same read and write calls work on files, pipes, terminals and sockets, and name the ways a socket genuinely differs from a file.

blocks.text: You have used file descriptors since the first module of the operating systems course. A socket is one too — the same small integer, the same read and write, the same close. That uniformity is deliberate, and it is why a program can be pointed at a file or a network connection without changing the code that moves the bytes.
One interface, many kinds of thing

rows: Bytes from disk, at your current position

blocks.text: Every one of those is read with read() and written with write(). A program that copies its input to its output works on all four without knowing which it has — which is exactly what makes shell pipelines from the Linux course composable, and what lets a network service be tested by pointing it at a file.

blocks.caption: The same code, three sources
lines: ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);

rows: End of file is near, or you asked for more than remains
Only part has arrived so far — more may follow
The other end closed its side
No position; bytes arrive once and are consumed

blocks.title: The bug this causes, in almost every first network program
blocks.text: Code that treats a socket like a file assumes one read returns the whole message. On a file that is usually true. On a socket it is not: a 1000-byte message may arrive as 500 and 500, or as 1 and 999, with no warning and no error. The fix is a loop that reads until it has what it needs — and the fact that this bug is invisible on a local connection and appears in production is exactly why it is worth knowing now, before you write the code.
TCP is a byte stream, not a message queue

This is the same point stated from the protocol's side. TCP guarantees that the bytes you send arrive in order and without gaps. It does not preserve where one write ended and the next began. Three writes of 100 bytes may be read as one block of 300, and one write of 300 may be read as three blocks.

items: If you need message boundaries, the protocol on top must create them
Fixed length: every message is the same size
Length prefix: send the size first, then that many bytes — the most common approach
Delimiter: end each message with a marker, as HTTP does with a blank line
Whatever you choose, the receiver must handle a message split across reads and two messages in one read

blocks.text: Descriptors are inherited, and that matters

The process module showed that a child inherits open descriptors across fork, which is how shell redirection works. The same applies to sockets, and it has a consequence worth knowing: a server that forks a worker per connection must close the listening socket in the child and the connection socket in the parent, or descriptors accumulate and a closed connection is never actually released.

blocks.caption: The close pattern for a forking server
lines: close(listener);      /* the child does not accept new connections */
close(conn);              /* the parent is done with this one */
/* Miss either close and the descriptor stays open in the wrong process. */

blocks.title: Treat four kinds of thing the same way
steps: Write a program that reads from descriptor 0 in a loop and writes to descriptor 1 until read returns 0
Run it with a file: ./copy < data.txt
Run it in a pipeline: cat data.txt | ./copy | wc -c
Run it interactively and end with Ctrl-D — that is what makes read return 0
Now point your own program at a socket instead of a file. In one terminal start a listener that just discards what it receives: nc -l 9000 > /dev/null
In another terminal, feed your program's output into it: ./copy < bigfile | nc localhost 9000
The point is that ./copy did not change at all — the same read and write calls work on a socket, because both are file descriptors
Run: ls -l /proc/self/fd     in a shell and identify what each descriptor points at
For a running server: ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | head    and count its open sockets
Run: ss -tnp | grep <pid>    and match the sockets against the descriptors
blocks.expected: One program that works on a file, a pipe, a terminal and a socket without modification, and a running process whose descriptors you can enumerate and identify. The last two commands are how you diagnose a descriptor leak in production — a count that only grows is the signature.

cheatsheet: A socket is a file descriptor: same read, write and close
One program can therefore work on files, pipes, terminals and sockets unchanged
On a socket, a short read is normal and means more may follow
read returning 0 on a socket means the other end closed its side
TCP preserves order and completeness, not message boundaries
If you need messages, add fixed length, a length prefix, or a delimiter
The receiver must handle one message split across reads and two messages in one read
Descriptors are inherited across fork — close the ones each side does not need
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd shows what a process has open; a growing count is a leak

checkpoint.prompt: Your program sends a 1000-byte message over TCP. The receiver's first read returns 500 bytes. What happened?

choices.C: Nothing wrong — TCP is a byte stream, so the rest may arrive on a later read

checkpoint.explanation: Order and completeness are guaranteed; boundaries are not. Loop until you have the number of bytes your protocol says to expect.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can the same read() and write() work on a file, a pipe, a terminal and a socket?

choices.B: The C library detects the type and adapts
choices.C: It only works if the sizes match
choices.D: They are all files on disk underneath

checkpoint.explanation: The kernel presents one interface over different kinds of object. That uniformity is what makes shell pipelines composable and lets the same program be pointed at a file or a connection without changing the code that moves bytes.

checkpoint.prompt: read() returns 0 on a socket. What does that mean?

choices.C: The other end closed its side of the connection

checkpoint.explanation: On a file it means end of file; on a socket it means the peer performed an orderly close. 'No data yet' on a blocking socket makes read wait rather than return 0.

checkpoint.prompt: A forking server's descriptor count grows steadily and never falls. What is the likely cause?

choices.D: The parent is not closing the connection descriptor after forking

checkpoint.explanation: It stays open in both processes. The child inherits every open descriptor. Each side must close what it does not need, or the connection is never fully released and the count only rises.
